stage_description: The juvenile stage runs from about 4 months to 1 year. Ferrets reach close to adult size by around 4 months and become sexually mature, though most pet ferrets are already neutered. This is often the peak of boisterous, curious energy: juveniles are confident, mischievous, and endlessly playful as growth finishes and their temperament settles.
nutrition: Continue a high-protein, high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet, transitioning from kitten formula toward a quality adult ferret food as growth completes. Free-feed to suit their fast metabolism, keep fresh water available, and avoid sugary or high-fiber treats that a carnivore's gut is not built for.
activity: Provide several hours of supervised out-of-cage play every day in a ferret-proofed space, with tunnels, dig boxes, and foraging games. Keep up regular handling and a routine, and secure hazards such as small swallowable objects and gaps behind appliances.
veterinary_check_frequency: Complete the vaccination series and give the first annual boosters for canine distemper and rabies, along with a yearly wellness exam. Discuss parasite prevention and confirm neuter status with an exotics or ferret vet.
dental_care: By now the permanent carnivore teeth, including the prominent canines, are all in. Start a regular tooth-brushing routine with a pet-safe paste; crunchy kibble or whole-prey items help slow the build-up of tartar.
warning_signs: Watch for signs of intestinal blockage — vomiting, no stool, straining, or sudden lethargy — as well as refusing food, persistent diarrhea, or laboured breathing. Any of these warrants a prompt visit to an exotics vet.
